questions.q: What does Windows Authentication Mode accept?
options: Only Windows logins — SQL Server logins are rejected outright, even if one exists
Neither — it requires a third-party authentication provider
Both Windows and SQL Server logins
Only SQL Server logins
questions.explain: This mode is exclusively Windows-based, rejecting SQL Server Authentication attempts entirely.

options: Only SQL Server logins
Both Windows logins and SQL Server logins
Only Windows logins
Only logins from a specific domain
questions.explain: Mixed Mode's formal name is 'SQL Server and Windows Authentication Mode' — both are accepted.

questions.q: Is there a mode that accepts only SQL Server logins and rejects Windows ones?
options: Yes, but only in cloud-hosted SQL Server instances
Yes, it's called SQL Server Authentication Mode
No — Windows Authentication is always available in both modes
This depends on the SQL Server edition
questions.explain: The only two modes are Windows Authentication Mode and Mixed Mode — there's no SQL-Server-only mode.

questions.q: Why might an organization choose Windows Authentication Mode alone?
options: It's the only mode that supports stored procedures
It's generally more secure for an all-Windows environment, centralizing credentials in Active Directory
It's the only mode that allows more than one user to connect
It's required for using transactions
questions.explain: This avoids managing a second, separate set of credentials outside Active Directory.

questions.q: What happens if a server is in Windows Authentication Mode only and someone tries to connect with a SQL Server login?
options: It works fine, since Mixed Mode is always enabled by default
The connection fails outright, regardless of whether the username/password are correct
SQL Server automatically converts it to a Windows login
The connection succeeds, but with limited permissions
questions.explain: The mode itself blocks the attempt before credentials are even checked.
